New York City Council: a first look at local ideal points

Pooled stated-meeting roll calls, 2022–2026 · Preliminary R analysis

Published

September 14, 2026

New York’s Council roll calls reveal a recognizable political spectrum. The DSA-endorsed members and much of the Progressive Caucus cluster at one end; the five Republicans form a sharply separated endpoint, with the bipartisan Common-Sense Caucus between them and the rest of the chamber. The same ordering appears in major disputes over policing, jail confinement, and rental broker fees, and it is strongly associated with 2024 presidential voting across the 51 council districts.

Dataset

The roll calls come from Jacob Greene (2026), MyTown: an open corpus of US and Canadian local-government meetings, decisions, and roll-call votes, CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.57967/hf/9676. The analysis uses the member_votes, municipalities, meetings, people, and people_aliases Parquet tables from the Hugging Face main dataset, downloaded September 14, 2026. Preserved local extracts define this analysis; no repository commit was pinned.

Coverage and construction

The extract contains 127,142 member-vote records from 94 stated meetings between January 5, 2022 and August 13, 2026. It covers 67 people because the period crosses council terms and includes replacements as well as current members. The main figure below marks the 51 members on the current official roster; former members remain in the pooled model so that overlapping service connects the scale across time.

Measure Value
Member-vote records 127,142
Stated meetings 94
Coverage January 5, 2022–August 13, 2026
Reconstructed vote events 2,518
Events with yea and nay 594
Events with at least two members on each side 346
Events retained for the main fit 339
Usable yea/nay votes 16,286
Members on the pooled scale 67

Each distinct meeting–motion combination is treated as a vote event. Yea is coded 1 and nay 0; absence, abstention, and unobserved entries are missing. The culling rule removes votes that do not meaningfully distinguish coalitions: it requires at least two members on each side and at least 40 recorded yea/nay votes. Unanimous, nearly unanimous, and thinly observed motions may matter substantively, but they carry little information about relative voting positions and can make a pooled estimate less stable. Seven of the 346 two-sided events fail the coverage threshold, leaving 339 contested roll calls.

Results

Council ideal points

An ideal point is a one-dimensional summary of voting similarity. Members placed near one another tend to take the same side on contested roll calls; members far apart tend to oppose one another. The units are relative to this New York sample and are not directly comparable to the numerical Chicago or Denver scores. The left-to-right labels describe the observed coalitions rather than imposing an ideological definition on the model.

Model specification, initialization, identification, diagnostics, and a repeated-pattern sensitivity check are in the self-contained technical appendix.

Individual members and policy controversies

The current-member endpoints are Tiffany Cabán (-1.49) and Alexa Avilés (-1.46) on the progressive side, and Vickie Paladino (2.46), Inna Vernikov (2.21), David Carr (2.18), and Joann Ariola (2.17) on the other. Former members Charles Barron and Kristin Richardson Jordan extend the pooled scale farther left; former Speaker Joseph Borelli extends it slightly farther right.

Three high-profile roll calls make that separation concrete. In January 2024, the Council overrode Mayor Eric Adams’s vetoes of the How Many Stops Act and a ban on solitary confinement, each by 42–9. The former requires reporting on lower-level police investigative encounters: supporters cast it as transparency and accountability after stop-and-frisk, while opponents argued that additional paperwork would divert officers from public safety. The latter limits isolation in city jails and adds procedural protections: supporters emphasized the physical and psychological harms of solitary confinement, while the mayor and other opponents argued that the restrictions would endanger correction officers and incarcerated people. The nine no votes in the MyTown roll calls form a compact positive-end coalition: Ariola, Borelli, Carr, Holden, Marmorato, Paladino, Vernikov, Yeger, and Zhuang. Council account of the override; official meeting agenda

The November 2024 FARE Act produced almost the same eight-member opposition coalition. Sponsored by Chi Ossé, the measure requires the party hiring a rental broker to pay the fee. Supporters argued that tenants should not face large upfront charges for a broker representing the landlord; brokers and real-estate groups warned that the cost could be folded into rents and disrupt their industry. The Council passed it 42–8, with Cabán, Avilés, Ossé, and the rest of the DSA bloc on the prevailing side and the scale’s Republican endpoint voting no. Council account of the FARE Act; Associated Press account of the controversy

These votes show why the scale is best described as running from a socialist/progressive pole to a moderate/conservative Democratic and Republican pole. It is not merely a party score: most Democrats occupy the middle, and the Common-Sense Democrats are visibly closer to the Republican end.

2024 presidential vote by council district

The analysis aggregates the New York Times published 2024 precinct polygons and results to the official 2023 council-district boundaries, then matches each district to the member serving on Election Day. The precinct data contain 1,903,342 Harris votes and 838,837 Trump votes within the five boroughs. The presidential source documents New York’s results and boundaries as official. New York Times precinct-data documentation; NYC council-district boundary dataset

Trump’s two-party share is strongly associated with council position: Pearson’s correlation is 0.72 across all 51 districts. A ten-percentage-point increase in Trump share corresponds to 0.37 ideal-point units in a simple bivariate regression (R² = 0.53). National partisanship does not explain every member—Districts 19, 30, 41, and 44 are visible exceptions—but it supplies an independent ordering that closely resembles the roll-call scale.

Political groupings

The following memberships are external classifications, not labels inferred from the votes. For comparability across cities, one DSA category is constructed from organizational election endorsements: NYC-DSA endorsed Cabán and Avilés in 2021 and re-endorsed both in 2025. A separate organizational measure captures the current officeholder bloc: Ossé and Hanif joined Cabán and Avilés in the four-member DSA City Socialist in Office bloc in 2026 without having won their seats with NYC-DSA endorsements. The distinction is meaningful institutionally—campaign endorsement versus post-election coordination—but modest empirically because all four occupy the same broad end of the roll-call scale.

The official Council lists 23 Progressive Caucus members and five Republicans on its 51-member roster. The six-member bipartisan Common-Sense Caucus contains Republicans Carr, Morano, and Vernikov and Democrats Mealy, Wong, and Zhuang; Ariola and Paladino left it in March 2026. Progressive Caucus 23 -0.61 0.45
Common-Sense Caucus 6 1.33 -0.21
Republican 5 2.16 -0.27

All five comparisons point in the expected direction. The two DSA-endorsed members occupy the negative endpoint, and adding Ossé and Hanif to form the four-member officeholder bloc changes little substantively. The broader Progressive Caucus also lies well to the left of members outside it. Republicans are the most positive group, and the Common-Sense Caucus sits toward that end even though half of its current members are Democrats. These are descriptive checks on the substantive meaning of the fitted dimension, not causal estimates or claims that every middle-ranked member has the same politics.

What this pilot shows

New York provides the clearest validation of the four city pilots so far. A one-dimensional roll-call model recovers known organizational groupings, the coalitions on salient public-safety and housing measures, and the partisan geography of council districts. The broad endpoints are persuasive; uncertainty and overlapping intervals still make fine-grained rankings in the Democratic middle less useful than the overall structure.
